## TL;DR

Fixed the directory fingerprinting gap found in review pass 17. The check and
handoff snapshots now share one Git-aware helper that verifies a directory is
its own repository before reading its revision. Uninitialized gitlinks use the
object id recorded by the parent index, initialized submodules include their
working-tree status, and unborn nested repositories remain representable. Added
regression coverage for those cases, corrected the check history documentation,
and documented the symlink-target limitation. The changed-main check passed
after formatting the implementation.

## Work and rationale

The latest review identified a specific boundary error in both the standalone
check snapshot and handoff snapshot. Running `git -C <directory> rev-parse
HEAD` does not prove that the directory is a repository: for an empty
uninitialized submodule directory, Git can resolve the parent repository's
HEAD. That made otherwise irrelevant bookkeeping commits appear to move the
submodule fingerprint. In the opposite direction, fingerprinting only a
submodule's HEAD missed edits to files inside an initialized submodule. A nested
repository with no commits also needed a stable fingerprint instead of being
treated as an unreadable state.

I added `gitDirectorySnapshot` in the core layer and wired both check.ts and
handoff.ts to it. The helper compares the real path reported by
`rev-parse --show-toplevel` with the directory being fingerprinted before it
uses repository-local information. If the directory is an initialized
repository, the fingerprint includes its permission mode, HEAD (or the
well-defined unborn state), and `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all`.
That makes a dirty file change the snapshot even when the submodule commit does
not. If Git resolves the directory to its parent, the helper checks the parent
index and records a gitlink's object id, which is available even when the
submodule has not been initialized. If there is no index entry and the
directory contains a `.git` marker but cannot establish its own repository
boundary, fingerprinting returns unknown so the caller fails closed.

The regression tests cover a clean initialized gitlink, an uninitialized
gitlink remaining unchanged after a parent bookkeeping commit, dirty content
inside an initialized submodule, and an untracked nested repository with no
commits. The nested-repository test checks both the normal tracked-source
snapshot and the shared directory helper, because Git enumerates an untracked
nested repository differently from a tracked gitlink. Existing symlink
coverage remains in place.

The reviewer also found duplicated, misplaced prose in
docs/check-run-history.md. I removed the extra appended heading and added the
directory behavior beside the existing gate drift explanation. Both that
history and user-docs/check.md now explain submodule status and the parent-index
gitlink fingerprint. They also state that symlinks are compared by their link
text and that changes to targets outside the worktree are not followed.

## Approaches tried

The first focused test run exposed an incorrect test assumption: Git reports
files under an untracked nested repository as untracked files, so the parent
snapshot did not necessarily contain a key exactly equal to the nested
directory. I changed the test to assert that the snapshot succeeds and records
the nested path, while calling the directory helper directly to verify the
unborn-repository fingerprint. The focused check-gate-bookkeeping suite then
passed.

I ran the requested `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. Its first pass
finished remote build, tests, UI smoke, and rendered contrast successfully but
failed the local format check. I ran `bun run fmt` and repeated the required
check. On that second run, the first remote host timed out and RepoOS retried
on another host. The retry completed successfully. Local guards, smoke,
rendered contrast, and the user-docs build also completed successfully.

## Challenges and blockers

The main technical challenge was distinguishing three cases that all look like
directories from the parent worktree: an initialized nested repository, an
uninitialized gitlink, and a nested repository that has not made its first
commit. A directory-local `HEAD` query alone cannot distinguish them safely.
The helper therefore establishes the repository root first, then uses the
parent index only for the gitlink case.

Remote validation was unusually slow. Each check encountered a hung
`thinkpad` validation container, which RepoOS removed and retried on `bee`.
Both retry behavior and the eventual successful gate result were observed in
the check output. The first check's only reported failure was formatting, which
was corrected before the passing run.

## Key learnings

Git commands run with `-C` can succeed from a directory that is not itself a
repository, so success from `rev-parse HEAD` cannot establish the repository
boundary. For nested repositories, snapshots need to record both revision and
working-tree status. For uninitialized gitlinks, the parent index is the
reliable source of the expected object id. When a repository marker exists but
Git cannot provide a trustworthy fingerprint, returning unknown lets the
existing fail-closed behavior protect the check result.

The tests also showed why the shape of Git's untracked path listing matters:
untracked nested repositories may be represented through their contained paths
rather than the directory entry itself. Tests should verify the observable
contract at the layer that owns each behavior, instead of assuming Git emits a
particular path shape.
